title: Goldman's Wilson picks two trades: US megacap tech and German fiscal winners
body: The positioning data is the standout for traders. With hedge fund net exposure near the bottom of its multi-year range, a benign CPI print (preview) or a breakthrough in the Iran conflict could force investors back into stocks quickly, amplifying any rally. In Europe, the strong inverse link between equities and Bund yields means an energy-driven inflation scare would hit stocks and bonds together, so gas storage heading into winter matters as much as the oil price for European equities. The French-German bond spread is set to remain a barometer of euro-area political risk into next year's presidential election, with the potential to weigh on the euro and French banks. Oil and gas remain the key swing factors for whether Europe's discount narrows. --- Goldman's Wilson sees investors who have cut risk to the bone facing a market where earnings are still growing fast and valuations have already come down.

title: UBS sees 28% Q3 S&P 500 earnings growth, says AI and cyclicals can lift US stocks
body: UBS's call gives investors a reason to look past this week's chip-led selling. With semiconductors expected to deliver around half of index earnings growth, results from chipmakers and hyperscalers are the main test of the bullish view. The bank's sector read favours industrials and AI-linked names over freight-heavy retailers and travel stocks, where energy costs bite hardest. Oil is the key risk. A further spike tied to Gulf escalation would widen the margin squeeze for goods sellers and test UBS's view that the hit to overall profits stays limited. Today's US CPI report is the near-term hurdle, since a hot core reading would push yields higher and weigh on richly valued tech. --- Earlier: US CPI preview: 14 investment bank forecasters see energy lifting headline to 3.6%, core held near 0.2% --- UBS argues the AI boom and a sturdy economy can carry US profits, and stocks, through high oil prices and rising yields.

title: US CPI preview: 14 investment bank forecasters see energy lifting headline to 3.6%, core held near 0.2%
body: The headline jump is largely priced in, so the market reaction will hinge on core. A print at the top of the forecast range, around 0.24% or higher, would back the Fed officials warning that inflation is broadening and firm December hike pricing, lifting front-end yields and the dollar. A reading at the soft end, near 0.16% to 0.18%, would support New York Fed President Williams' view that price pressures are shock-driven and could trim expectations for tightening beyond this year. For oil, the report is a reminder that crude is now feeding straight into US inflation through gasoline. Any renewed spike in prices from Gulf escalation would show up in next month's headline and keep energy at the centre of the Fed debate. --- Earlier: US CPI: Energy prices expected to lift headline inflation. title: How to read a whale alert: an Ethereum case study and a 5-point checklist
body: How to read an on-chain whale alert before you react: an Ethereum case study Early this week, an on-chain tracker reported that two wallets "linked to the Ethereum Foundation" had deposited 4,393 Ether (ETH), about $11.1 million, into the Kraken exchange. The post asked whether the Foundation was "dumping ETH again". Early Ethereum Foundation ETH recipients move $11M to Kraken: what the data shows ETH fell 3.6% the following day, which seemed to support that reading. A day later it had recovered almost all of the loss. Alerts like this one appear daily, and markets can react to them quickly. A few simple checks show how much an alert actually tells you. Here are five of them, applied to this week's example. 1. Understand what trackers can see, and what they can't Every transfer on a public blockchain such as Ethereum is visible: which address sent coins, which address received them, how many, and when. Analytics platforms such as Arkham Intelligence and services such as Lookonchain turn that data into readable alerts. Trackers can't see who owns an address unless it has been identified, and they can't see what happens inside an exchange. Once coins reach an exchange deposit address, any sale happens on the exchange's internal order book, which is not recorded on the blockchain. In this case: the blockchain confirms that the coins reached Kraken. It does not show whether they were sold. 2.

title: ICYMI - Three Fed officials signal inflation fight continues; Williams sees no 2027 hike
body: With October largely priced out, Tuesday's trio keeps December in focus for the next move. Williams' comments on 2027 cap how far markets can push expectations for the peak rate. That should limit the upside for longer-dated Treasury yields and the dollar unless the data turns. Barkin's warning that shocks are continuing gives the hawkish camp an opening if inflation stays sticky. Oil is the swing factor. Williams' benign outlook assumes energy won't add to inflation next year, so a renewed crude surge, for example from escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites, would undercut that view and strengthen the case for more tightening. For now, oil is effectively a direct input into Fed pricing. --- Three Fed voices agree the inflation fight isn't over; the open question is whether today's shocks fade on their own or keep the Fed hiking into 2027.

title: Oil Extends Gains on Mideast Escalations
body: Crude oil rose toward $95 per barrel on Wednesday, extending its rally to a fifth straight session as escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi rebels heightened fears of supply disruptions in the Middle East. On Tuesday, Yemen's Houthi militants fired a missile at Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, in eastern Saudi Arabia, igniting a fire in part of the complex. The rebels had also targeted Riyadh's main airport over the weekend, while a Saudi-led coalition mounted an offensive to recapture rebel-held territory in Yemen. At the same time, Tehran has stepped up attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, though the United States said it had helped facilitate the passage of more than 19 million barrels of crude through the strategic chokepoint. In Europe, President Trump defended his diesel export agreement with Russia, arguing that the additional supplies would flow into the global market and help alleviate elevated prices. title: NZX 50 Extends Losses, Tracking Wall Street Lower
body: The NZX 50 fell 48 points, or 0.4%, to 13,702 in Wednesday morning trade, extending the previous session's losses and mirroring an overnight decline on Wall Street led by weakness in major semiconductor stocks. Sentiment was cautious ahead of the release of China's September CPI, PPI, and trade data later today, amid subdued domestic demand and higher oil prices. Investors were also awaiting key US inflation figures for guidance on the Federal Reserve's upcoming interest rate decision, alongside New Zealand's food inflation and business PMI data due later this week. At the same time, markets continued to track developments in the Middle East—particularly the Saudi Arabia–Houthi conflict—and their potential impact on crude prices. Sector-wise, financials, energy, technology, and consumer discretionary stocks were the main drags on the index. Notable decliners included AFT Pharmaceuticals (-2.0%), Infratil (-1.8%), Briscoe Group (-1.8%), Freightways Group (-1.5%), Summerset Group (-1.2%), Meridian Energy (-0.9%), Channel Infrastructure (-0.9%), and A2 Milk (-0.6%). title: New Zealand Tourist Arrivals Rise Least in 3 Months
body: Visitor arrivals to New Zealand rose 8.0% year-on-year to 248,714 in August 2026, easing from an 8.5% increase in July and marking the slowest pace of growth in three months. Arrivals from China recorded the largest gain, up by 6,500, followed by Australia (up 5,800), the United States (up 2,000), and Malaysia (up 1,300). Several markets achieved record August arrival numbers, including Australia (125,600), Taiwan (5,800), and Singapore (4,600). Overall, overseas visitor arrivals recovered to 99% of pre-pandemic levels, compared with 251,100 in August 2019. Australians remained the largest visitor group, accounting for 51% of total arrivals, followed by China (11%), the United States (6%), and Japan (4%), underscoring the continued rebound in international tourism demand. body: New Zealand's tourism sector showed fresh momentum in the latest data release, with visitor arrivals rising 2.8% month-over-month as of 13 October 2026. The figures are based on a month-over-month comparison, where the current reading reflects the change in visitor arrivals for the latest month versus the prior month, while the previous 0.5% figure measured the change in that earlier month against its own preceding period. The shift from modest growth to a more robust 2.8% suggests improving travel conditions and potentially stronger support for New Zealand's tourism-dependent industries, including hospitality, retail, and transport. Market participants and policymakers will be watching upcoming releases to see whether this uptick in arrivals consolidates into a sustained trend, which could bolster broader economic activity and improve revenue streams in key tourist hubs across the country. title: Argentina Inflation Rises in September
body: Argentina's consumer price index increased by 1.9% month-on-month in September 2026, up from 1.7% in August, bringing cumulative inflation for the year to 23.6%. The largest monthly rise was recorded in housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels (3.1%), followed by education (3.0%). Restaurants and hotels registered the smallest increase at 1.1%, while clothing and footwear climbed 1.4%. Food and non-alcoholic beverages were the main driver of monthly inflation in all regions except Greater Buenos Aires, where housing and utilities exerted the greatest impact. Core CPI rose 1.7%, supported in part by higher prices for dining out and pharmaceutical products. Seasonal prices advanced 2.9%, led by vegetables, tubers and legumes, while regulated prices rose 2.3%, reflecting higher gas, electricity and private healthcare tariffs. title: Ibovespa Drops as Inflation Forecast Rises
body: The Ibovespa fell 1% on Tuesday, closing at 206,887 points, pressured by declines in major banks, utilities, and mining stocks. The Focus survey raised its 2026 inflation forecast to 5.22% from 5.01%, the fourth consecutive upward revision, while the Selic benchmark interest rate remained unchanged at 13.25%. The IMF cut its 2026 GDP growth forecast for Brazil to 2.2% from 2.4%, citing an expected slowdown in 2026–2027 driven by restrictive interest rates designed to bring inflation back to target, the withdrawal of fiscal stimulus, and heightened global uncertainty. Among financials, major banks moved lower, with Itaú down 1.6% and Bradesco off 1%. In the utilities segment, Axia retreated 1.6%, while Sabesp slipped 3.1%. Mining stocks also weakened, as ample global supply, elevated Chinese inventories, and lower shipping costs continued to pressure iron ore prices, pulling Vale down 1.1%. Moving against the broader trend, Petrobras advanced 1.5% as oil prices rebounded. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: TSX Rises as Banks and Energy Stocks Advance
body: The S&P/TSX Composite Index rose 0.9% to close at 35,984 on Tuesday, supported by stabilizing Canadian bond yields. The pause in the recent bond selloff, which had driven yields to multi-year highs, lifted credit-sensitive sectors, particularly financials. Among the major banks, RBC gained 1.3%, TD Bank advanced 2.2%, BMO rose 1.3%, and both Scotiabank and CIBC added 1.8%. Energy stocks also moved higher as oil prices recovered from earlier losses. Canadian Natural climbed 4.8%, Suncor added 3.7%, Imperial Oil gained 4.5%, and Cenovus advanced 4.2%. In the technology sector, Shopify and Constellation Software each rose 3%, buoyed by strength in US hyperscalers, while Celestica slid 1.7%, mirroring weakness among semiconductor names. Elsewhere, CSG acquired a 9.5% stake in MDA Space, becoming its largest shareholder; MDA shares rose 1.1% on the news. Miners lagged as gold prices declined.
